Also in-thread: the owner adds the command: and command-edit: bind-value prefixes so keybindings can invoke arbitrary commands without a dedicated plugin function.

Merged PR #3518 reworks CursorPageUp/Down (and SelectPageUp/Down) to be nano-like: adds a new pageoverlap setting (default 2) so paging keeps that many lines visible across the page boundary, replacing the old jump-to-top/bottom-of-view behavior. Review surfaced real design tradeoffs worth keeping: scrollmargin vs pageoverlap are deliberately kept separate (users may want scrollmargin 0 but still want paging overlap, or vice versa); the fix must scroll/clamp using only the first cursor (Cursor.Num == 0) to avoid multiplied scrolling under multicursors, since these actions are still listed in MultiActions; and Relocate() still applies scrollmargin after paging, which the maintainers decided is correct (matches vim's scrolloff behavior on page up/down) rather than forcing the cursor to the exact edge like plain nano.

Open draft PR #3733 adds a new `micro/overlay` Lua package (CreateOverlay/DestroyOverlay/DrawText/DrawRect/BufPaneScreenLoc/GetColor/StringToStyle/Redraw) letting plugins paint arbitrary widgets over the screen each frame, plus two example plugins (completebox, an autocomplete popup; quickmenu, a find/grep palette) that establish an immediate-mode event-handling idiom (track_event registers a preX/onX global hook, event() polls whether it fired since the last redraw, reset between frames) to work around there being no focus-capture mechanism. Real open design tensions surfaced in review: the terminal cursor is drawn on top of overlays with no fix yet beyond the stalled hidecursor option (#2632), which is buffer-local and thus awkward for non-buffer-bound overlays; overlay.StringToStyle's freeform "extra fg,bg" string format is called out as a bad API that should maybe be dropped in favor of GetColor; and there is no official way for Lua to query usable screen geometry, so plugin authors are stuck computing it by hand from InfoBar's view (worked around with a ScreenSize() helper posted in-thread) because maintainer dmaluka confirms screen.Redraw() is deliberately not exposed (plugin code never runs outside the main loop, so there's no async case needing it) and overlay.Redraw() only forces an immediate repaint since Lua state changes otherwise show up only on the next natural redraw.

Owner explains why macOS Cmd cannot be a micro modifier: micro only ever receives whatever key events the terminal emulator decides to forward, and terminals reserve Cmd combinations for their own keybindings (new tab, quit, etc.) rather than sending them through to the running program, so there is no escape sequence for micro to bind to; Cmd-V often appears to work only because the terminal's own paste binding injects the clipboard text as a stream of ordinary key events, and Cmd-C does not copy because the terminal has no knowledge of micro's internal selection state.

Explains why copy-to-local-clipboard is fundamentally limited over SSH: micro runs remotely with no access to the local X11/system clipboard, so Ctrl-C/Ctrl-Shift-C only populates micro's internal (or the remote X) clipboard. Owner states there are exactly two fixes: disable micro's mouse option so the local terminal itself handles mouse selection and its own copy keybinding (shift+mouse-click forces terminal-native selection even with mouse on, per a widely-thumbsupped workaround), or use a terminal supporting the OSC52 escape sequence with micro's `clipboard` option set to `terminal`, which lets micro request/set the clipboard through the terminal protocol instead of the OS directly. useprimary/mouse interact non-obviously (useprimary false plus mouse on still breaks remote copy) which confused multiple reporters before landing on the mouse-off or OSC52 workaround.

The Linux virtual console (TERM=linux) sends no escape sequences at all for Shift/Ctrl+Arrow combos, so Shift-Left/Right selection silently fails to mark a selection; the owner's fix is two-sided: a loadkeys kmap (reproduced in the thread, originally adapted from the tilde project) that remaps console keycodes to emit standard xterm-style sequences like \033[1;2C (Shift-Right) and \033[1;5D (Ctrl-Left) via /etc/console-setup/remap.inc on Debian-based systems, plus a corresponding change on micro's side so it recognizes those sequences specifically when TERM=linux rather than requiring the user to fake TERM=xterm (which breaks other console apps' own escape handling, e.g. F3/F4 in mc). The kmap only persists per-boot via loadkeys, not per-login, which confused multiple reporters; the final combined fix is documented on the project wiki.

Closed/superseded (by #1762) PR that nonetheless records the real design debate behind hlsearch (highlight-all-matches): this version hooked into the syntax Highlighter by dynamically adding/removing regex "custom patterns" overlaid on top of syntax highlighting, and exposed a generic bp:HighlightCustomPattern(group, regex) Lua method (reusable for things like highlighting trailing whitespace, not just search) with ToggleHighlightSearch as a bindable action. Owner zyedidia pushed back that reusing the syntax highlighter couples hlsearch to syntax-highlighter internals and ignores the search's actual range/case-sensitivity; dmaluka's counter-proposal (landed in the superseding #1762) was a LineArray-based approach that recomputes matches during BufWindow display rather than mutating the Highlighter, after measuring that redoing the regex search on every display call is CPU-expensive enough on real files to reject that "just search every time" alternative. Also surfaced: the quick syntax-highlighter hack had a sharing bug where multiple BufPanes on the same Buffer leaked each other's search highlights because Highlighter state lives on the buffer, not the pane.

Long-running feature request for softwrap-at-a-fixed-column (the exact feature this repo's colwrap plugin project targets); only workaround found pre-fix was a manual/Lua-automated vertical split sized to the desired width, which is fragile against terminal startup resize races (#1800) and was abandoned by the requester as too distracting. The issue records a concrete design proposal (posted under this requester's own account) for a new `softwrapcolumn` integer common option: default 0/off, clamped to pane width, orthogonal to wordwrap, deliberately decoupled from colorcolumn (which stays a pure visual guide), with over-length single words still hard-breaking exactly as today's edge-wrap does; continuation rows still start at column 0 so cursor/visual-position mapping is untouched. Critically, the cross-references show PR #4142 ("Add softwrapcolumn option to soft-wrap at a fixed column") already closes this issue — i.e. this capability has since landed upstream in micro's Go core, which conflicts with this repo's current working assumption that no such built-in option exists; #4142 should be checked directly before any further plugin/fork design work proceeds.

Merged PR #1981 is the softwrap architecture rewrite still underpinning micro's current internal/display/softwrap.go and bufwindow.go: View.StartLine changes from a plain line number to an SLoc{Line, Row} pair (Row = visual row within a wrapped buffer line), and all vertical scrolling (ScrollUp/Down, Center, PageUp/Down, Relocate, End) is rebuilt on top of BufWindow.Scroll(SLoc, n)/Diff(SLoc, SLoc)/SLocFromLoc(Loc), with a getRow/getRowCount helper computing how many visual rows a line occupies from w.Width - w.gutterOffset (minus 1 for the scrollbar). This SLoc plumbing, and the fact that bufWidth/gutterOffset remain unexported and are exactly what getRow divides by, is the concrete mechanism behind this repo's documented constraint that softwrap's wrap width is derived from pane geometry rather than a Lua-settable option. Also notable: the PR explicitly scopes out word wrap and cursor up/down-within-wrapped-line as deliberate followups (landed later in #2076), and flags as a known separate bug that `v.Height` callers don't account for the statusline row.

On Windows terminals other than plain cmd.exe (PowerShell, mintty/Cygwin/Babun), micro can fail at startup with "No suitable screen available" and exit; the trigger is having TERM (e.g. "xterm") or MICRO_TRUECOLOR set in the environment, which pushes tcell's Windows backend down a termios-based code path tcell simply does not implement on Windows (tcell's tscreen_windows.go has no termios support), so it errors out instead of falling back to the native Windows console API. Workarounds in the thread: unset TERM/MICRO_TRUECOLOR entirely (loses truecolor support as a tradeoff), or for mintty specifically run micro via `winpty micro` (loses mouse input as a tradeoff). No real fix landed; a maintainer later asked in 2024 whether it's still reproducible on recent versions without getting an answer.

Merged PR #3540 fixes a regression where CursorDown/CursorPageDown ignored a selection whose end sits at column 0 (i.e. includes the trailing newline), landing on: when deselecting such a selection, Cursor.Deselect(false) now lands exactly on CurSelection[1] instead of one character before it (removing a `.Move(-1, ...)`), and CursorDown/CursorPageDown special-case selectionEndNewline to call Cursor.Start() rather than moving down an extra line. The harder, explicitly unresolved design question the review surfaces: micro hides the terminal cursor and does not highlight the current line (or its ruler number) while a selection is active, so "where does Down land after deselecting" has no single right answer the way it would in a GUI editor that still shows an I-beam cursor during selection (nano, gnome-text-editor, VS Code all keep the cursor visible); the maintainers explicitly declined to add a compensating extra move-right/down to mimic those editors, accepting the resulting asymmetry (e.g. CursorPageDown can leave the cursor one line short of the buffer end when selecting near EOF) as acceptable given micro's different cursor-visibility model. Also fixes a reappeared bug where the current-line highlight could still trigger for a cursor with an active selection.
